activities.topic: Introduction to Machines and Basic Robotics Concepts

activity_1.title: Find a Smart Machine Around You
steps: Look around your house, farm, or village.
Find at least three machines that help people do work.
Observe what work each machine is doing.
Think about how these machines make work easier.
Relate these machines to everyday tasks.

activity_2.title: Observe How It Works
steps: Choose one machine and observe it carefully.
Identify what information the machine receives.
Think about what decision happens after receiving the input.
Observe what action the machine performs.
Relate this process to input, decision, and action.
examples: Water motor: input is switching ON, action is water flowing
Torch: input is pressing switch, action is light turning ON

extra_exploration.task: Look around your village and find machines that help people work faster and observe how they reduce effort.
examples: Electric street light turning ON at night

think_and_notice: Which machine in your village helps people save time or effort?
What happens when someone presses a switch or button?
How do machines help farmers or workers complete their work faster?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your ideas with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify machines used in rural life
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe technology used in farms and villages.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand how machines help humans
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize how machines reduce human effort.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and analytical skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how machines start and perform work.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real life
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand how robots are advanced machines designed to help people.

bonus_activity: Ask an elder in your house how work was done before machines like tractors or motors were used.
Listen carefully and compare it with how machines are used today.
Think about how machines have changed people's work and made tasks easier.

activity_1.title: Find a Tool or Machine
steps: Look around your house or farm.
Find one tool or machine made of multiple parts.
Observe the machine carefully.
Identify different parts that help it work.
Think about how these parts are connected.

activity_2.title: Identify the Parts
steps: Choose one machine to study in detail.
List the different parts of the machine.
Observe how each part contributes to the machine.
Think about how the parts work together.
Relate this to a system where each part has a role.
examples: Bicycle: wheels, chain, pedals, handle, seat
Ceiling fan: blades, motor, switch, rod

extra_exploration.task: Find more objects made of connected parts and observe how each part performs a specific function.

think_and_notice: What parts did you observe in the machine?
Which part helps the machine move?
Which part helps control the machine?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize systems made of multiple parts
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how machines are built from many components.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand the role of different parts
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify that each part performs a specific function.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and analytical skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how machines around them operate.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real life
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand that robots are also built using many coordinated parts.

bonus_activity: Ask someone at home which machine in your village has the most parts.
Examples may include tractor, bicycle, or flour mill.
Try to count and list as many parts as you can identify in that machine.

activities.topic: Gripping Mechanisms and Basic Robotic Movement

activity_1.title: Pick and Move Objects
steps: Find three small objects in your house.
Use only your thumb and index finger to pick each object.
Lift the object and place it somewhere else.
Observe how your fingers hold and release the object.
Think about how grip strength and control work together.

activity_2.title: Try a Simple Grab Tool
steps: Take two sticks, pencils, or spoons.
Hold them like a pair of tongs.
Try picking up small objects using the sticks.
Observe how the tool helps in gripping objects.
Compare this with how your fingers work.

extra_exploration.task: Find tools used for picking or holding objects and observe how they help improve grip and control.
examples: Farming tools used to lift objects

think_and_notice: Which method made it easier to pick up objects?
How do your fingers work together to hold something tightly?
Why do machines sometimes use robotic arms to pick objects?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand gripping mechanisms
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how objects can be held and moved using simple tools.

learning_outcomes.title: Relate human hand movement to robotic arms
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand how robots mimic human hand functions.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and motor coordination skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how grip and movement work together.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real-world tools
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify tools that use similar gripping mechanisms.

bonus_activity: Look around your house and find three tools that help people lift or hold objects.
Examples include pliers, tongs, and farming tools.
Observe how these tools increase human strength and control, similar to robotic arms.

activities.topic: Grip Strength and Robotic Claw Mechanisms

activity_1.title: Test Your Grip Strength
steps: Collect three different objects from your home.
Hold each object tightly using your hand.
Observe which objects are easy to hold.
Notice which objects are difficult to hold.
Think about how size and shape affect grip.

activity_2.title: Use a Simple Tool to Grab
steps: Take two spoons, sticks, or pencils.
Hold them together like a pair of tongs.
Try picking up small objects using the tool.
Observe how the tool improves your grip.
Compare this with using your hand directly.

extra_exploration.task: Find tools used for gripping or holding objects and observe how they help apply strong and stable grip.
examples: Farm tool used to lift bundles

think_and_notice: Which object was easiest to grab and hold?
How did the sticks or spoons help you grip objects better?
Why do machines sometimes need strong claws to hold objects?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand gripping mechanisms
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how objects can be held using different methods.

learning_outcomes.title: Relate human tools to robotic claws
learning_outcomes.description: Students understand how robots mimic tools used by humans.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and coordination skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how grip strength affects holding objects.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real-world tools
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize how gripping mechanisms are used in everyday tools.

bonus_activity: Look around your house or farm and find three tools that help people hold, grab, or lift objects.
Examples include pliers, tongs, and farming tools.
Think about how a robotic claw could perform the same work automatically.

activity_1.title: Lift Different Weights
steps: Find three objects with different weights from your house.
Lift each object using one hand.
Observe which objects are easy to lift.
Notice which objects are heavy to lift.
Think about how weight affects the effort needed.

activity_2.title: Use a Tool to Lift
steps: Take a long stick, ruler, or wooden spoon.
Place a small object on the ground.
Use the stick to push and lift the object.
Observe how the tool reduces effort.
Relate this to how machines help lift heavy objects.

extra_exploration.task: Find machines or tools that help lift heavy objects and observe how they reduce human effort.
examples: Hand pulley used to pull water from a well

think_and_notice: Which object was most difficult to lift?
How did the stick help you move or lift objects?
Why do machines use mechanisms to lift heavy things?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your observations with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand lifting mechanisms
learning_outcomes.description: Students observe how objects can be lifted using tools.

learning_outcomes.title: Recognize how machines increase human strength
learning_outcomes.description: Students identify how tools and machines help lift heavy loads.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and reasoning skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students analyze how different objects require different effort to lift.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real-world machines
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate robotic lifting mechanisms to machines used in daily life.

bonus_activity: Ask an elder how heavy objects were lifted before machines were used.
Examples may include manual lifting, pulley systems, or wooden carts.
Think about how robots or machines could make this work easier today.

activity_1.title: Find Objects With Different Roles
steps: Look around your house or farm.
Collect or observe five different objects.
Identify different parts of each object.
Observe how each part helps the object work.
Think about the role of each part.

activity_2.title: Group the Parts by Their Work
steps: Choose one machine or object you observed.
List its different parts.
Group the parts into power source, movement parts, and structure parts.
Observe how each group has a different function.
Relate this grouping to how machines are designed.
examples: Movement parts: wheels, rotating parts, pedals

extra_exploration.task: Find machines with multiple connected parts and observe how each part performs a specific role.

think_and_notice: Which machine had the most parts?
Which parts help the machine move?
Which parts help the machine stay strong and stable?
activities.discussion_instruction: Discuss your ideas with your parents or elders.

learning_outcomes.title: Understand that machines are made of many parts
learning_outcomes.description: Students recognize that machines consist of components with specific roles.

learning_outcomes.title: Identify different functions of parts
learning_outcomes.description: Students classify parts based on their function such as movement, power, and structure.

learning_outcomes.title: Develop observation and analytical skills
learning_outcomes.description: Students carefully examine machines and tools around them.

learning_outcomes.title: Connect robotics concepts with real-life machines
learning_outcomes.description: Students relate everyday machines to how robots are built.

bonus_activity: Ask someone which machine in your village has the most parts.
Examples may include tractor, flour mill, or bicycle.
Try to list at least five parts of that machine.
